title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
summary: Buy and sell as often as you like, holding at most one share at a time. Return the maximum profit.
statement:
`prices[i]` is the price of a stock on day `i`. You may buy and sell as many times as you like, but you can hold at most one share at a time (you may sell and buy again on the same day).

Return the maximum profit.
hints: Any profitable stretch can be split into day-to-day rises.
Add up every positive difference prices[i] − prices[i − 1].
The general method, two states (holding / not holding) updated each day, extends to the harder variants.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Transaction Fee
summary: Trade as often as you like (one share at a time), paying fee per completed transaction. Return the maximum profit.
statement:
`prices[i]` is the price of a stock on day `i`. You may make as many transactions as you like, holding at most one share at a time, but every transaction (a buy followed by a sell) costs `fee`.

Return the maximum profit.
hints: Small rises are no longer worth trading on: the fee eats them.
Track two states: cash (not holding a share) and hold (holding one).
Each day: cash = max(cash, hold + price − fee), hold = max(hold, cash − price). Use the old values on the right-hand side.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock III
summary: Complete at most two transactions (sell before buying again). Return the maximum profit.
statement:
`prices[i]` is the price of a stock on day `i`. You may complete at most two transactions, and you must sell before you buy again.

Return the maximum profit.
hints: Model the stages: after the first buy, after the first sell, after the second buy, after the second sell.
buy1 = max(buy1, −price); sell1 = max(sell1, buy1 + price); buy2 = max(buy2, sell1 − price); sell2 = max(sell2, buy2 + price).
Start buy1 and buy2 at negative infinity (or −prices[0]) and the sells at 0. The answer is sell2.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV
summary: Complete at most k transactions (sell before buying again). Return the maximum profit.
statement:
`prices[i]` is the price of a stock on day `i`. You may complete at most `k` transactions, and you must sell before you buy again.

Return the maximum profit.
hints: Generalise the two-transaction solution to k pairs of states: buy[j] and sell[j] for j = 1 … k.
Each day: buy[j] = max(buy[j], sell[j − 1] − price) and sell[j] = max(sell[j], buy[j] + price).
If k ≥ n / 2, the limit never matters, so just add every rise as in "Stock II". That avoids a large table.

title: Student Attendance Record II
summary: Records of length n use A (absent), L (late) and P (present). Count the records with fewer than 2 A in total and never 3 or more consecutive L, modulo 10^9 + 7.
statement:
An attendance record is a string of length `n` using `A` (absent), `L` (late) and `P` (present). A record is eligible for an award if it has fewer than 2 `A`s in total and never has 3 or more consecutive `L`s.

Return the number of eligible records of length `n`, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
hints: A record is described well enough by two numbers: how many A's so far (0 or 1), and how many L's at the very end (0, 1 or 2).
That is 6 states. Appending P, A or L moves between them: P resets the trailing Ls, A requires 0 A's so far, L requires fewer than 2 trailing Ls.
Update the 6 counts n times, modulo 10⁹ + 7, and add them up. Matrix exponentiation would make it O(log n).

title: Beautiful Arrangement
summary: Count permutations of 1..n where, at every 1-indexed position i, perm[i] is divisible by i or i is divisible by perm[i].
statement:
A permutation `perm` of the numbers `1` to `n` is beautiful if, for every position `i` (1-indexed), `perm[i]` is divisible by `i` or `i` is divisible by `perm[i]`.

Return the number of beautiful permutations.
hints: Build the permutation position by position and prune as soon as a placement breaks the rule.
Backtracking with a "used" array is fast enough for n ≤ 15.
For a DP version, let the state be the set of numbers used (a bit mask). The next position is the count of bits set plus 1.

title: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets
summary: Return whether the array can be split into k non-empty subsets with equal sums.
statement: Return `true` if the values of `nums` can be divided into `k` non-empty groups whose sums are all equal. Every value must be used exactly once.
hints: Each group must sum to total / k. If that is not an integer, or some value is larger than it, return false.
Bit-mask DP: for each mask of used values, store the sum of the bucket currently being filled (total of mask modulo target). A value can be added if it fits in that bucket.
A backtracking alternative fills buckets one at a time, trying values in descending order and skipping equal choices.

title: Minimum Number of Work Sessions to Finish the Tasks
summary: A work session lasts at most sessionTime hours and a task can't be split across sessions. Return the fewest sessions to finish every task (any order).
statement:
`tasks[i]` is the number of hours task `i` takes. You work in sessions of at most `sessionTime` hours each. A task must be finished within a single session, but you can do tasks in any order.

Return the minimum number of work sessions needed to finish all the tasks.
constraints: Every task fits in a session: max(tasks) ≤ sessionTime
hints: With at most 14 tasks, you can afford a state that records which tasks are done: a bit mask.
For each mask, store the best pair (sessions used, hours used in the current session).
From a mask, add a task: if it fits in the current session, add its hours; otherwise start a new session. Keep the lexicographically smallest pair.

title: Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes
summary: In a connected undirected graph (graph[i] lists i's neighbours), return the length of the shortest walk that visits every node. You may start and end anywhere and revisit nodes and edges.
statement:
`graph` is a connected undirected graph with `n` nodes, where `graph[i]` lists the neighbours of node `i`. Return the length (number of edges) of the shortest walk that visits every node.

You may start and end at any node, and you may revisit nodes and reuse edges.
constraints: The graph is connected and has no self-loops
hints: The position alone is not enough as a state: you also need to know which nodes have been visited.
Run BFS over states (node, mask of visited nodes), starting from every (i, 1 << i) at once.
The first time you reach a state whose mask has every bit set, its distance is the answer.

title: Find the Shortest Superstring
summary: Return a shortest string that contains every word as a substring (no word contains another). Any shortest answer is accepted.
statement:
Return a shortest string that contains every string in `words` as a substring. No word is a substring of another.

If several shortest strings exist, any of them is accepted.
constraints: No word is a substring of another
hints: Placing word b right after word a saves the length of the longest suffix of a that is a prefix of b. Precompute that overlap for every pair.
The task becomes finding the order of words that maximises the total overlap: a travelling-salesman style problem.
DP over (mask of words used, last word) storing the best total overlap and the parent choice, then rebuild the string by following the parents.
